config.whisper_disfluency_prompt: Um, so I was, uh, I was thinking that maybe we could, you know, we could try... I mean, it's, it's not really, hmm, how do you say it, it's not really that simple, right? Like, uh, the thing is, the thing is that I, I don't, I don't know.

structures.label: Future: will
structures.example: I think it will take about three months.

use: decisions made right now, on the spot
predictions and promises without a plan behind them
offers: I'll take care of it
examples: I'll call you back in five minutes.
This won't work, trust me.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't use it for things already arranged - that's 'going to' or present continuous.

structures.label: Future: going to
structures.example: We are going to move in September.

use: plans and intentions decided before speaking
predictions based on what you can see now
examples: We're going to rewrite this module.
Look at those clouds - it's going to rain.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't say 'will' for a plan you already have - 'I will move next month' sounds like you just decided.

structures.label: Future continuous
structures.example: This time next week I will be sitting on a train.

use: an action in progress at a specific future moment
polite questions about someone's plans: will you be using this?
examples: At nine I'll be driving, so text me instead.
Will you be joining the call?
cheatsheet.mistake: Not for completed future results - 'by Friday I will be finishing' should be 'I will have finished'.

structures.label: Future perfect
structures.example: By June I will have finished the migration.

use: something completed BEFORE a future deadline
usually with 'by': by Monday, by the end of the year
examples: By June we'll have migrated everything.
She'll have left before you arrive.
cheatsheet.mistake: If there is no deadline in the sentence, you probably want plain 'will'.

structures.label: Past simple
structures.example: I left at seven and got there late.

use: finished actions at a known time: yesterday, in 2020, last week
sequences of events in a story - one thing after another
examples: I pushed the fix and went home.
The meeting ended at noon.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't use present perfect with a finished time: 'I have seen him yesterday' is wrong.

structures.label: Past continuous
structures.example: I was reviewing the code when the call came.

use: background action interrupted by a shorter event
what was in progress at a specific past moment
examples: I was reviewing the code when the server died.
At 8 pm we were still debugging.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't narrate whole stories in it - the events that move the story forward take past simple.

structures.label: Past perfect
structures.example: The deadline had already passed when I noticed.

use: the earlier of two past events - the 'past of the past'
often with: by the time, already, before, when I realized
examples: By the time I checked, the deadline had passed.
I realized I had sent the wrong file.
cheatsheet.mistake: Unnecessary when the order is already clear from 'before/after' - past simple is enough.

structures.label: used to
structures.hint: used to + infinitive, for discontinued states and habits
structures.example: I used to commute two hours a day.

use: past habits and states that are no longer true
contrasting then vs now
examples: I used to commute two hours a day.
There used to be a shop here.
cheatsheet.mistake: 'I am used to getting up early' is a different structure (be used to + -ing) - it means accustomed, not a past habit.

structures.label: would (habitual past)
structures.hint: would + infinitive for repeated past actions
structures.example: Every summer we would drive to the coast.
structures.detect: would + VB in past narrative context

use: repeated past actions in storytelling, usually after the scene is set
pairs well with: every summer, as a child, back then
examples: Every Friday we would order pizza and ship a release.
My dad would read to me every night.
cheatsheet.mistake: Only actions, never states - 'I would live in Berlin' is wrong, use 'used to live'.

structures.label: Zero conditional
structures.example: If a meeting has no agenda, it runs long.

use: things that are always true - rules, habits, cause and effect
'if' means 'whenever' here
examples: If a meeting has no agenda, it runs long.
If I skip lunch, I get grumpy.
cheatsheet.mistake: No 'will' anywhere - that would turn it into a prediction about one specific case.

structures.label: First conditional
structures.example: If the build fails, I will roll it back.

use: real, likely future situations and their results
warnings, plans, negotiations
examples: If the build fails, I'll roll it back.
If you finish early, we'll grab lunch.
cheatsheet.mistake: Present tense after 'if' - never 'if it will rain'.

structures.label: Second conditional
structures.example: If I had more time, I would rewrite it.

use: unreal or unlikely present/future - imagining things
polite suggestions and hypotheticals: what would you do?
examples: If I had more time, I'd rewrite it.
If she lived closer, she'd visit more.
cheatsheet.mistake: Never 'would' in the if-clause: 'if I would have time' is the classic error.

structures.label: Third conditional
structures.hint: if + had + past participle, would have + past participle
structures.example: If I had asked earlier, I would have saved a week.
structures.detect: if + had + VBN, would|could|might + have + VBN

cheatsheet.form: if + had + p.p., would have + p.p.
use: past that did NOT happen and its imagined past result
regrets, post-mortems, lessons learned
examples: If I had asked earlier, I would have saved a week.
If we'd tested it, the bug would have been caught.
cheatsheet.mistake: 'If I would have known' - wrong; the if-clause takes 'had known', never 'would'.

structures.label: Mixed conditional
structures.example: If I had studied law, I would be in a different city now.
structures.detect: if + had + VBN, would + VB (present reference)

cheatsheet.form: if + had + p.p., would + verb (or reversed)
use: past cause with a PRESENT result: a decision then, a situation now
present cause with a past result: if I knew him, I would have called him
examples: If I had studied law, I'd be in a different city now.
If he had saved money, he wouldn't be broke today.
cheatsheet.mistake: Watch which half is past and which is present - 'now/today' signals the present half.

structures.label: Speculation: present
structures.example: She must be stuck in traffic.

cheatsheet.form: must / might / may / could / can't + be
use: guessing about now: must = almost sure, might/may/could = possible, can't = impossible
examples: She must be stuck in traffic.
That can't be the right address.
cheatsheet.mistake: The opposite of 'must be' is 'can't be', not 'mustn't be'.

structures.label: Speculation: past
structures.hint: must / might / could have + past participle
structures.example: He might have forgotten the meeting.

cheatsheet.form: must / might / could / can't + have + p.p.
use: guessing about the past: what probably happened
post-mortems and detective work: the cache must have expired
examples: He might have forgotten the meeting.
She must have taken the earlier train.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't drop 'have': 'he must forgot' is wrong.

structures.label: Passive voice
structures.example: The parts are assembled in three factories.

use: when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant
processes and systems: the parts are assembled in three factories
keeping the topic in the subject position
examples: The decision was made without me.
The invoice will be sent tomorrow.
cheatsheet.mistake: Don't force it when the doer matters - 'the bug was introduced by me' is weaker than 'I introduced the bug'.

structures.label: Reported speech
structures.example: He said he had already sent it.

use: relaying what someone said - tense usually steps one back: is->was, will->would, did->had done
'tell' needs a person, 'say' does not
examples: She said she was leaving the company.
He told me the project had been canceled.
cheatsheet.mistake: 'He said me' - wrong; either 'he told me' or 'he said to me'.

structures.label: Relative clauses
structures.hint: who / which / whose / that, defining and non-defining
structures.example: The colleague whose desk faces the window never uses it.

use: packing two sentences into one: identifying people and things
who = people, which = things, that = both (informal), whose = possession
examples: The engineer who wrote this left last year.
I met a woman whose brother runs the bakery.
cheatsheet.mistake: No double subject: 'the tool which we use it daily' - drop the 'it'.

structures.label: Gerund vs infinitive
structures.hint: verb patterns: avoid doing, plan to do, keep doing, refuse to do
structures.example: I keep postponing it because I refuse to admit it is stuck.

use: -ing after: enjoy, avoid, keep, finish, suggest, mind
to + verb after: decide, agree, plan, refuse, manage, want
remember/stop/try change meaning depending on which one follows
examples: I enjoy reading before bed.
He decided to sell the car.
cheatsheet.mistake: 'I enjoy to read' - wrong; when unsure, learn the verb together with its pattern.

structures.label: wish / if only
structures.hint: wish + past for present regret, wish + past perfect for past regret
structures.example: I wish I had said no at the start.

use: present regrets: wish + past simple (I wish I had more time)
past regrets: wish + past perfect (I wish I had taken the job)
'if only' = the same, but stronger
examples: I wish it were summer already.
If only we had started earlier.
cheatsheet.mistake: Not 'I wish I have' - wish always pushes the tense one step back.
